{{Short description|Class of stochastic processes in applied probability}}
[[File:Warehouse md17.jpg|thumb|Regenerative processes have been used to model problems in inventory control. The inventory in a warehouse such as this one decreases via a stochastic process due to sales until it gets replenished by a new order.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Hurter | first1 = A. P. | last2 = Kaminsky | first2 = F. C. | doi = 10.1287/opre.15.3.467 | title = An Application of Regenerative Stochastic Processes to a Problem in Inventory Control | journal = Operations Research | volume = 15 | issue = 3 | pages = 467–472 | year = 1967 | jstor = 168455}}</ref>]]
In [[applied probability]], a '''regenerative process''' is a class of [[stochastic process]] with the property that certain portions of the process can be treated as being [[statistically independent]] of each other.<ref name=Ross2>{{Cite book | last1 = Ross | first1 = S. M. | chapter = Renewal Theory and Its Applications | doi = 10.1016/B978-0-12-375686-2.00003-0 | title = Introduction to Probability Models | pages = 421–641 | year = 2010 | isbn = 9780123756862 }}</ref> This property can be used in the derivation of theoretical properties of such processes.

==History==
Regenerative processes were first defined by [[Wally Smith (mathematician)|Walter L. Smith]] in [[Proceedings of the Royal Society A]] in 1955.<ref>{{Cite journal
| last1 = Schellhaas | first1 = Helmut
| doi = 10.1287/moor.4.1.70
| title = Semi-Regenerative Processes with Unbounded Rewards
| journal = [[Mathematics of Operations Research]]
| volume = 4
| pages = 70–78
| year = 1979
| jstor = 3689240}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Smith | first1 = W. L. | author-link1 = Wally Smith (mathematician)| title = Regenerative Stochastic Processes | doi = 10.1098/rspa.1955.0198 | journal = Proceedings of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences | volume = 232 | issue = 1188 | pages = 6–31| year = 1955 |bibcode = 1955RSPSA.232....6S }}</ref>

==Definition==
A '''regenerative process''' is a [[stochastic process]] with time points at which, from a probabilistic point of view, the process restarts itself.<ref name=Ross>{{cite book|title=Introduction to probability models|author=Sheldon M. Ross|isbn=0-12-598062-0|page=442|year=2007|publisher=Academic Press}}</ref> These time point may themselves be determined by the evolution of the process. That is to say, the process {''X''(''t''),&nbsp;''t''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;0} is a regenerative process if there exist time points 0&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''T''<sub>0</sub>&nbsp;<&nbsp;''T''<sub>1</sub>&nbsp;<&nbsp;''T''<sub>2</sub>&nbsp;<&nbsp;... such that the post-''T<sub>k</sub>'' process {''X''(''T<sub>k</sub>''&nbsp;+&nbsp;''t'')&nbsp;:&nbsp;''t''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;0}

* has the same distribution as the post-''T''<sub>0</sub> process {''X''(''T''<sub>0</sub>&nbsp;+&nbsp;''t'')&nbsp;:&nbsp;''t''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;0}
* is independent of the pre-''T<sub>k</sub>'' process {''X''(''t'')&nbsp;:&nbsp;0&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''t''&nbsp;<&nbsp;''T<sub>k</sub>''}

for ''k''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;1.<ref name="haas">{{Cite book | first1 = Peter J. | last1 = Haas|author-link= Peter J. Haas (computer scientist)| doi = 10.1007/0-387-21552-2_6 | chapter = Regenerative Simulation | title = Stochastic Petri Nets | series = Springer Series in Operations Research and Financial Engineering | pages = 189–273 | year = 2002 | isbn = 0-387-95445-7 }}</ref> Intuitively this means a regenerative process can be split into [[independent and identically distributed|i.i.d.]] cycles.<ref name=applied>{{Cite book | first1 = Søren | last1 = Asmussen| doi = 10.1007/0-387-21525-5_6 | chapter = Regenerative Processes | title = Applied Probability and Queues | series = Stochastic Modelling and Applied Probability | volume = 51 | pages = 168–185 | year = 2003 | isbn = 978-0-387-00211-8 }}</ref>

When ''T''<sub>0</sub>&nbsp;=&nbsp;0, ''X''(''t'') is called a '''nondelayed regenerative process'''. Else, the process is called a '''delayed regenerative process'''.<ref name="haas" />

==Examples==
*[[Renewal process]]es are regenerative processes, with ''T''<sub>1</sub> being the first renewal.<ref name=Ross/>
*Alternating [[renewal process]]es, where a system alternates between an 'on' state and an 'off' state.<ref name=Ross/> 
*A recurrent [[Markov chain]] is a regenerative process, with ''T''<sub>1</sub> being the time of first recurrence.<ref name=Ross/> This includes [[Harris chain]]s.
*[[Reflected Brownian motion]] is a regenerative process (where one measures the time it takes particles to leave and come back).<ref name=applied/>

==Properties==
*By the [[renewal reward theorem]], with probability 1,<ref name=sigman>Sigman, Karl (2009) ''Regenerative Processes'', lecture notes</ref>

::<math>\lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{1}{t}\int_0^t X(s) ds= \frac{\mathbb{E}[R]}{\mathbb{E}[\tau]}.</math>

:where <math>\tau</math> is the length of the first cycle and <math>R=\int_0^\tau X(s) ds</math> is the value over the first cycle.

*A [[measurable function]] of a regenerative process is a regenerative process with the same regeneration time<ref name=sigman/>
